extracted.intended_audience: EPA decisionmakers, regulatory attorneys, agency scientists, and public commenters on the Endangerment Finding rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and scientific public comments evaluating EPA's proposed rescission of the Endangerment Finding under the Clean Air Act, focusing on the adequacy of the agency's factual and scientific reasoning and reliance on supporting reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: More detailed justification required when new policy contradicts prior policy (Fox v. Allentown)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new policy rests upon factual findings that contradict those which underlay an agency's prior policy, the agency must provide a more detailed justification for the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Fox, 556 U.S. at 515. The proposal’s three-and-one-half pages purporting to evaluate thousands of pages of scientific evidence are inadequate; overturning an existing Endangerment Finding requires fuller explanation and reasoned analysis than provided here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot rely arbitrarily on a deeply flawed report
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency's reliance on a single, substantively and procedurally flawed report (here, the Draft CWG Report) to support rescission is arbitrary and illegal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both substance and process (see Comment VIII). Where the draft report is incomplete, misrepresentative, or methodologically unsound, agency reliance on it fails the requirement of reasoned decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residual uncertainties cannot justify declining an Endangerment Finding (Massachusetts v. EPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Residual uncertainties in the science do not permit EPA to decline to find that greenhouse gases endanger public health or welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Massachusetts v. EPA, 549 U.S. 497, 534 (2007), the types of 'residual uncertaint[ies]' raised by the proposal are insufficient as a legal basis for rescission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific assessments must be comprehensive and not omit important lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A credible assessment must comprehensively review the relevant scientific literature and not entirely ignore important independent lines of evidence documenting harms from climate change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Draft CWG Report admits it is not comprehensive; that is insufficient when an agency relies on it. Examples of omitted evidence include already observed negative impacts on crops, marine food sources, species and ecosystems, wildfire risk, disease patterns, water supply, and human health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where a report addresses a topic, it must acknowledge and address substantial contradictory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a report includes some discussion of a topic, it must also consider and address substantial additional scientific evidence that contradicts its conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Draft CWG Report in some chapters fails to address literature contradicting its conclusions (e.g., ocean warming, ocean deoxygenation, species range shifts, plant responses to elevated CO2, phenology shifts). Agency reliance requires engagement with that literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not misrepresent findings or present information in a manner designed to mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: An assessment or proposal must not misstate or selectively present scientific findings in a way that obfuscates the true state of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of misrepresentation include unjustified claims about misuse of RCP8.5, mischaracterizing ocean pH trends (e.g., comparing unrelated locations/times), overstating differences between observations and models, overstating uncertainty in climate sensitivity, using selective geographies to downplay hurricane trends, and choosing metrics to claim a lack of trends in extreme precipitation and heatwaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim topics or arguments are new or overlooked when they were already considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments presented as novel or previously overlooked must in fact be new; otherwise the claim is misleading if prior literature already examined and rejected them or if models already incorporate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include alternative Total Solar Irradiance records, RCP8.5 critiques, CO2 fertilization discussions, Urban Heat Island considerations, and variability in local sea level—these have been examined in the literature or accounted for in climate models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting irrelevant uncertainties to sow doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting scientific uncertainties that have no bearing on the central question (whether GHGs endanger health/welfare) to create doubt is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Report points to known uncertainties (e.g., an unresolved driver of post-Pinatubo CO2 decrease or model representation of hemispheric albedo) without drawing conclusions, apparently to cast doubt; an agency must explain how such uncertainties affect the endangerment determination if it intends to rely on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline scientific findings EPA must recognize
rubrics_metrics.description: Any credible agency position must be consistent with the established scientific understanding summarized in EPA’s 2022 denial of petitions: six core conclusions about greenhouse gases and climate change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those key points are: (1) anthropogenic emissions are raising atmospheric GHG concentrations to unprecedented levels; (2) accumulation of GHGs exerts a warming effect; (3) warming is unequivocal across multiple observations; (4) anthropogenic emissions are the primary driver of recent warming; (5) without substantial emissions reductions, concentrations and rates of change will increase; and (6) threats to public health and welfare will likely mount as GHGs accumulate. Any attempted rescission must grapple with and justify departure from these findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate treatment of greenhouse gas concentrations and global temperature attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments must accurately reflect the consensus that human influences are causing dangerous and rapid increases in CO2 and other GHGs and that other forcings (e.g., TSI, UHI) are comparatively minimal and already accounted for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that factors like Total Solar Irradiance or Urban Heat Island effects explain observed warming are wrong unless plausibly demonstrated; studies and detection/attribution literature account for these factors and still identify radiative forcing from GHGs as dominant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect is a localized, largely accounted-for factor, not a global driver
rubrics_metrics.description: UHI has relatively small global impact and the scientific community accounts for it in temperature analyses; it cannot explain global warming trends, especially in remote and oceanic regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistical adjustments and specialized datasets exclude or adjust urban data; fastest warming areas are remote (Arctic/Antarctic) and oceans (majority of Earth's surface) show warming in satellite and sea-surface temperature records—so UHI cannot overturn attribution to GHGs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total Solar Irradiance (TSI) alternatives do not overturn anthropogenic attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of TSI record or claims about solar forcing do not change the overall weight of evidence that anthropogenic GHGs are the primary cause of recent warming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative TSI reconstructions claimed to be overlooked have been examined in the literature and found implausible; even different TSI choices cannot reproduce observed warming without anthropogenic forcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct interpretation and use of emissions scenarios (RCPs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emissions scenarios like RCP8.5 are tools to compare a range of possible futures and are not predictions of the most likely outcome; criticizing prior work for using RCP8.5 as 'business as usual' misstates its intended role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCP8.5 is a high-end scenario reflecting high population and slow technological progress. IPCC and the scenario authors describe it as 'very high' emissions; agency analyses must be transparent about scenario assumptions and cannot discredit impacts shown under lower-emissions scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency discussions must be sufficiently detailed to evaluate extensive scientific evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A cursory few pages cannot responsibly evaluate or overturn conclusions supported by thousands of pages of scientific literature and assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal’s brief Alternative Rationale (roughly three-and-one-half Federal Register pages) is inadequate to supplant the extensive scientific record; the agency must provide fuller, documented analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reports relied upon must disclose limitations and not be presented as comprehensive when they are not
rubrics_metrics.description: When a supporting report admits non-comprehensiveness (e.g., short timeline, technical complexity), an agency must account for those limitations rather than treating the report as a full scientific synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Draft CWG Report’s own acknowledgment that it could not comprehensively review all topics undermines its use as a primary basis for rescission unless EPA supplements it with comprehensive reviews and addresses the gaps.
